page_content: COMP64702 (Transforming Text Into Meaning) is taught by Prof. Chenghua Lin and Dr. Jingyuan Sun in the Computer Science Department at the University of Manchester. Lectures run on Mondays 10:00-12:00 weekly, and lab sessions run on Fridays 12:00-14:00 in weeks 3, 5, 7, and 9. Lecture slides for each week are released one week in advance and all materials are on Canvas. Assessment has two components, a team coursework and a final exam, each worth 50% of the overall module mark. Chenghua is responsible for the coursework and for running the labs. There are nine teaching assistants and a discussion forum on Canvas.

metadata.part: Part I: Introduction

page_content: The course aims to develop a solid understanding of text mining and NLP fundamentals such as text preprocessing and representations; to trace the evolution of language models leading to transformers and modern large language model architectures; to cover both traditional and state-of-the-art (transformer-based) approaches to core NLP tasks; to explain how large language models are trained and aligned through pre-training and instruction tuning; to evaluate and compare approaches to NLP tasks systematically; and to develop and apply, as a team, various NLP methods to extract information and meaning from large-scale textual data.

metadata.part: Part I: Introduction

page_content: Natural Language Processing (NLP) has traditionally focused on modelling linguistic structure and meaning, such as syntax, semantics, and discourse. Text Mining has traditionally focused on discovering patterns and useful information from large text collections, for example topic modelling. The two fields are increasingly converging: they share representations, models, and evaluation benchmarks, overlap strongly in statistical and neural language processing, and modern large language models blur the distinction between NLP and text mining.

metadata.part: Part I: Introduction

page_content: Text mining and NLP power many everyday applications. Machine translation systems such as Google Translate convert text between languages. Question answering assistants such as Amazon Alexa answer spoken questions about the weather, news, or reminders. Historical legal text analytics processes handwritten records such as the Aberdeen council registers, which run nearly continuously from 1398 to the present in Latin and Middle Scots. Fact checking verifies claims in social media posts. Data-to-text generation automatically produces reports such as weather forecasts from structured data. ChatGPT can answer questions, do mathematics, write songs, poems and emails, generate dialogue, generate and debug code, and complete text, marking a significant step toward artificial general intelligence.

metadata.section_title: Why Text Mining and NLP: Applications
metadata.part: Part I: Introduction

page_content: Text mining and NLP are challenging because natural languages evolve: new words appear constantly (for example 'emoji' or 'to DM'), syntactic rules are flexible ('Coming?' versus 'Are you coming?'), and ambiguity is inherent. Interpretation often requires world knowledge; for instance, understanding 'The player took three steps. The whistle blew.' relies on knowledge of sport. There are also many languages, dialects, and styles to handle.

metadata.section_title: Why Text Mining and NLP are Challenging
metadata.part: Part I: Introduction

page_content: Some languages present specific challenges. Chinese text has no spaces between words, so word segmentation is required and can be ambiguous: the same character sequence for 'Wuhan Yangtze River Bridge' can be mis-segmented as 'Wuhan / mayor / Daqiao Jiang'. Chinese is an ideographic language, unlike alphabetic English, and traditional Chinese characters carry much richer stroke signals than their simplified counterparts (for example the characters for love, horse, and noodle).

metadata.part: Part I: Introduction

page_content: Traditional rule-based or symbolic artificial intelligence requires expert knowledge to engineer rules and does not adapt well across languages, domains, and applications. Learning from data (machine learning) adapts to language evolution by simply learning from new data, and adapts to different applications by learning with the appropriate target representation.

metadata.section_title: Why Machine Learning for TM and NLP
metadata.part: Part I: Introduction

page_content: NLP is a confluence of computer science, artificial intelligence, and linguistics. Machine learning provides techniques for solving problems by learning from data and is the currently dominant AI paradigm, often used to model NLP tasks. NLP is related to but broader than Computational Linguistics (CL): in CL, computational methods support the study of linguistic phenomena and theories such as formal discourse theories, whereas NLP has a more general scope covering translation, information extraction, and question answering. The top NLP conference is the Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL)

page_content: Typical NLP applications include machine translation, sentiment analysis, information extraction, text summarisation, question answering, dialogue systems, and many more.

metadata.part: Part I: Introduction

page_content: A vector, also called an embedding, is a one-dimensional array of d elements or coordinates, each identified by an index i. A collection of n vectors forms a matrix X of size n by d, also called a vector space. Note that in Python indices start from 0. For example a vector x might be [2, 0, ..., 5], and a matrix stacks many such vectors as rows.

metadata.part: Part II: Vector Representations of Text

page_content: To measure how close two vectors are, we use similarity measures. The dot product (inner product) takes two equal-length vectors and returns a single number: the sum over each dimension of the products of corresponding coordinates. Cosine similarity normalises the dot product by dividing by the magnitudes (norms) of the two vectors, giving a value in the range 0 to 1 for non-negative vectors. The norm or length of a vector is the square root of the dot product of the vector with itself. Cosine similarity is preferred when the direction of the vector matters more than its length.

metadata.section_title: Vector Similarity: Dot Product and Cosine
metadata.part: Part II: Vector Representations of Text

page_content: For text data there are two classic ways to form a vector space. A word-word (term-context) matrix has words as both rows and columns and records how often words co-occur. A document-word (bag-of-words) matrix has documents as rows and vocabulary words as columns and records word counts per document. The choice of what forms the rows and columns determines what similarity we can compute.

metadata.part: Part II: Vector Representations of Text

page_content: We need vector representations of text for several reasons. First, to encode the meaning of words so we can compute semantic similarity between them, for example deciding whether basketball is more similar to football or to recipe. Second, for document retrieval, such as retrieving documents relevant to a query in web search. Third, to apply machine learning to textual data, because clustering and classification algorithms operate on vectors.

metadata.part: Part II: Vector Representations of Text

page_content: Before vectorising we define text units. A word (token or term) is a sequence of one or more characters excluding whitespace, and can sometimes be an n-gram. A document (text sequence or snippet) can be a sentence, paragraph, section, chapter, an entire document, a search query, a social media post, a transcribed utterance, or a pseudo-document such as all tweets posted by one user.

metadata.part: Part II: Vector Representations of Text

page_content: Tokenisation obtains tokens from raw text. The simplest form splits text on whitespace or uses regular expressions. For example, the sentence 'Lost Highway is a dark, violent, surreal masterpiece.' becomes the tokens 'Lost', 'Highway', 'is', 'a', 'dark', ',', 'violent', and so on, separating punctuation from words.

metadata.part: Part II: Vector Representations of Text

page_content: After tokenisation, other preprocessing steps may follow: lowercasing; removal of punctuation, numbers, stop words, and infrequent words; and stemming. For example, applying lowercasing and stop-word and punctuation removal to a movie review might reduce it to the informative words: concerned, lynch, best, lost, highway, dark, violent, surreal, beautiful, hallucinatory, masterpiece.

metadata.part: Part II: Vector Representations of Text

page_content: Given a corpus D of m preprocessed texts, such as a set of movie reviews or tweets, the vocabulary V is the set of all k unique words appearing in D, written V = {w1, ..., wk}. The vocabulary is often extended to include n-grams, which are contiguous sequences of n words.

metadata.part: Part II: Vector Representations of Text

page_content: The simplest word representation is a discrete one-hot vector. Given the text 'love pineapple apricot apple chocolate apple pie', the vocabulary is {apple, apricot, chocolate, love, pie, pineapple} with size 6. Each word becomes a vector that is all zeros except for a single 1 at its vocabulary position; for instance apricot = [0,1,0,0,0,0] and pineapple = [0,0,0,0,0,1]. This is known as one-hot encoding.

metadata.part: Part II: Vector Representations of Text

page_content: One-hot vectors have a fundamental problem. The dot product and cosine similarity of any two different one-hot vectors is zero, so every word is equally different from every other word. For example apricot and pineapple have cosine similarity 0 even though they are clearly related fruits. This motivates using contextual information to capture meaning.

metadata.part: Part II: Vector Representations of Text

page_content: The distributional hypothesis, associated with Firth (1957), states: you shall know a word by the company it keeps. Words appearing in similar contexts are likely to have similar meanings. The classic 'tesguino' example illustrates this: from sentences like 'A bottle of tesguino is on the table', 'Everybody likes an ice cold tesguino', 'Tesguino makes you drunk', and 'We make tesguino out of corn', we can infer that tesguino is a beer-like alcoholic drink made from corn, purely from its contexts.

metadata.part: Part II: Vector Representations of Text

page_content: A word-word or term-context matrix X is n by m, where n is the number of target words in the vocabulary V and m is the number of context words. For each target word we count how many times it co-occurs with each context word, using a context window of plus or minus k words to the left and right, computed over a large corpus such as all of Wikipedia. Usually the target and context vocabularies are the same, giving a square matrix. With such counts, apricot and pineapple end up with similar rows, so their cosine similarity becomes high (close to 1), while apricot and digital have similarity 0.

metadata.part: Part II: Vector Representations of Text

page_content: Contexts can be refined using linguistic information. For example, part-of-speech tags distinguish 'bank' as a verb from 'bank' as a noun, and syntactic dependencies distinguish 'eat' as a direct object relation from 'eat' as a subject relation. These richer contexts can produce more precise word representations.

metadata.part: Part II: Vector Representations of Text

page_content: A document-word matrix X is |D| by |V|, where rows are documents in the corpus and columns are vocabulary words. For each document we count how many times each vocabulary word appears. For example three movie reviews might have counts for the words bad, good, great, and terrible. This matrix can also be obtained by summing the one-hot vectors of the words in each document and transposing.

metadata.part: Part II: Vector Representations of Text

page_content: Raw counts have a problem: frequent words such as articles and pronouns dominate the contexts without being informative. For instance, adding the word 'the', which co-occurs with most nouns, can push the cosine similarity between two otherwise different words up to around 0.997. This effect applies to both the word-word and the document-word matrix. The solution is to weight the vectors so that informative words count for more.

metadata.part: Part II: Vector Representations of Text

page_content: One way to weight the word-word matrix is a distance discount: context words are weighted according to their distance from the target word, so the further away a context word is, the lower its weight. For a window of size plus or minus k, the context word at each position is multiplied by (k minus distance) divided by k; for k = 3 the weights are 1/3, 2/3, 3/3 immediately around the word, tapering off with distance.

metadata.part: Part II: Vector Representations of Text

page_content: Pointwise Mutual Information (PMI) measures how often two words occur together relative to how often they would occur independently. PMI of words wi and wj is the log base 2 of the joint probability P(wi, wj) divided by the product of the marginal probabilities P(wi) and P(wj), where probabilities are estimated from corpus counts. Positive PMI values quantify genuine relatedness and are used instead of raw counts. Negative values are usually ignored, giving Positive PMI (PPMI), defined as the maximum of PMI and 0.

metadata.part: Part II: Vector Representations of Text

page_content: TF-IDF represents the importance of a word in a document relative to a corpus. Term Frequency (TF) captures that a term appearing frequently in a document is likely important to that document. Inverse Document Frequency (IDF) captures that a term appearing in many documents is less informative as a distinguishing feature; IDF of word w is the log base 10 of N divided by df_w, where N is the number of documents and df_w is the number of documents containing w. The TF-IDF weight of word w in document d is its term frequency multiplied by its IDF.

metadata.part: Part II: Vector Representations of Text

page_content: Count-based matrices for words and documents often work well, but they are high dimensional, since the vocabulary can be millions of words, and very sparse, since words co-occur with only a few other words and documents contain only a small subset of the vocabulary. The solution is dimensionality reduction, which produces lower-dimensional dense vectors.

metadata.part: Part II: Vector Representations of Text

page_content: Word vectors can be evaluated intrinsically or extrinsically. Intrinsic evaluations include: similarity, ordering word pairs by their semantic similarity; in-context similarity, substituting a word in a sentence without changing its meaning; and analogy, such as 'Beijing is to China what Rome is to ...?'. Extrinsic evaluation measures whether the vectors improve performance on a downstream task such as sentiment classification or named entity recognition.

metadata.part: Part II: Vector Representations of Text

page_content: Which word vectors are best? High-dimensional count-based vectors are one option, and a later lecture shows how neural networks produce low-dimensional vectors. Levy, Goldberg and Dagan (2015) showed that choices such as context window size and rare-word removal matter more than the specific method. The choice of texts used to obtain the counts also matters: more text is better, and low-dimensional methods scale better.

metadata.section_title: Best Word Vectors and Practical Lessons
metadata.part: Part II: Vector Representations of Text

page_content: Word vectors have limitations. Polysemy means all occurrences and senses of a word share one vector, so it is often useful to adapt the vector to the appropriate sense, for example 'bank'. Antonyms appear in similar contexts and are hard to distinguish from synonyms. Compositionality is unresolved: obtaining the meaning of a sequence of words does not scale from short phrases to whole sentences or paragraphs. Partial solutions include combining word vectors by addition or multiplication, and models such as sentenceBERT.

metadata.part: Part II: Vector Representations of Text

page_content: Document vectors are evaluated intrinsically through document similarity and information retrieval, and extrinsically through tasks such as text classification and plagiarism detection. Their main limitation is that word order is ignored, even though language is inherently sequential.

metadata.section_title: Evaluation and Limitations of Document Vectors
